entry.title: Control variates for dry friction under colored noise: variance rates for non-smooth observables

link.title: Control variates for dry friction under colored noise: variance rates for non-smooth observables

entry.content: A control variate method was introduced by Garnier and Mertz (2022) for multivalued stochastic differential equations driven by colored noise. For smooth observables, the asymptotic variance is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$, where $\varepsilon^{2}$ is the correlation time of the noise. However, for non-smooth reliability observables, such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities, rate estimates have not been established in general. In this paper, rate estimates are derived for the inertial dry-friction inclusion driven by colored noise in the three regimes whose white-noise propagators are known. The asymptotic variance of the resulting control variate estimators is $O(\varepsilon^{2\alpha})$ for $\alpha$-H"older observables with $\alpha\in(0,1]$, $O(\varepsilon)$ for observables of bounded variation satisfying a one-sided continuity condition, $O(\varepsilon^{1+\alpha})$ for observables that are both $\alpha$-H"older and of bounded variation, and $O(\varepsilon^{\min{2,1+2\alpha}})$ for observables with finitely many $\alpha$-cusps, where $\alpha \in (0, 1]$ is the cusp exponent. The last three bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. Bounds on the bias of the white-noise approximation and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates are also derived, and the comparison principle is shown to be preserved under coupled time discretization. Numerical experiments in the three regimes support the predicted rates.

entry.title: Variance estimation for generalized linear regression with binary outcome when using case-cohort data

link.title: Variance estimation for generalized linear regression with binary outcome when using case-cohort data

entry.content: The case-cohort design was initially proposed for studying rare outcomes in large cohorts, where covariates may be too expensive to measure on all the subjects. Because of its sampling scheme, this design often requires intricate variance estimation. However, there is significantly less publications on the use of case-cohort data with binary outcomes than for case-cohort survival analysis, notably regarding inference. In this work, an influence-based variance estimation method is proposed for parameters obtained from log-linear or logistic regression models and case-cohort data. The approach is flexible and is illustrated on two cohort subsampling designs: (i) a design possibly stratified on some correlate of the covariates but where sampling of the cases is exhaustive; (ii) a design where the sampling is further stratified based on case status. The variance estimation method properly accounts for the sampling features and allows appropriate analysis of case-cohort data. It is illustrated on a simulation and on data from the National Wilms Tumor Study Group. Influences, and therefore variance estimates, can be easily computed from outputs of standard R commands such as glm and glmgee. In addition to being much less computationally intensive, influence-based variance estimation is more reliable than bootstrap variance estimation, recently proposed by Noma [Journal of Epidemiology, 2024].

link.title: Robust and Sparse Personalized Federated Learning via Gamma-Divergence

entry.content: To address the challenges of statistical heterogeneity across clients and within-client data contamination in federated learning, we propose a robust and sparse personalized federated learning method based on the gamma-divergence, termed Gamma-PFL. entry.title: Beyond the Mean: A Two-Stage GAMLSS Framework for Physical Activity Bout Patterns and Survival in COPD

link.title: Beyond the Mean: A Two-Stage GAMLSS Framework for Physical Activity Bout Patterns and Survival in COPD

entry.content: Physical activity patterns in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are typically summarised using simple metrics such as total daily activity or mean time spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. In many studies, this activity is further characterized through physical activity bouts, defined as periods of at least 10 consecutive minutes above 3 metabolic equivalent tasks (METs). However, such summaries overlook the highly skewed, heterogeneous and patient-specific nature of bout-related variables, which may contain clinically relevant information. We propose a distributional modelling approach for accelerometer-derived bout-related physical activity outcomes based on Generalised Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS). The framework models multiple parameters of the outcome distributions, including location, scale, and the probability of observing no bouts, allowing the analysis to extend beyond average levels of activity. In a second stage, the estimated distributional parameters are incorporated into a survival analysis to investigate whether information beyond the mean is associated with patient prognosis. The proposed framework is illustrated using accelerometer data from a cohort of 512 COPD patients and considering bout-related outcomes such as minutes accumulated in bouts per day, total number of bouts, and area under MET in bouts per day. The resulting distributional parameters were significantly associated with mortality and provided information beyond average activity levels, particularly through differences in variability across patients. These findings suggest that information contained in distributional parameters beyond the mean may be relevant for understanding the relationship between physical activity patterns and survival.

entry.title: Data-Driven Learning of Directed Acyclic Graphs in Gaussian Linear Structural Equation Models with Latent Variables

link.title: Data-Driven Learning of Directed Acyclic Graphs in Gaussian Linear Structural Equation Models with Latent Variables

entry.content: Structural equation modeling is typically performed in a confirmatory manner, requiring a priori specification of both the measurement model and the path diagram connecting the structural variables. In this paper, we study a semi-exploratory setting within a general Gaussian linear structural equation model with latent variables, where the loading structure in the measurement model is known, but the structural path diagram follows an unknown directed acyclic graph (DAG) to be learned from data. First, we establish the identifiability of the structural model, showing that the unknown DAG is identifiable only up to its Markov equivalence class. We then propose DAGGLE (\underline{D}irected \underline{A}cyclic \underline{G}raph learning in \underline{G}aussian \underline{L}inear structural \underline{E}quation models), a two-stage likelihood-based approach for simultaneous DAG structure learning and parameter estimation. In the first stage, we screen candidate edges via continuous optimization of a penalized marginal likelihood. In the second stage, we further prune the remaining edges using a BIC-guided backward search over the space of Markov equivalence classes. Under mild regularity and search conditions, DAGGLE recovers the true Markov equivalence class with probability tending to one. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive numerical simulations and an application to the European Social Survey (Trust in Justice module), where DAGGLE yields a model that aligns with substantive theory while improving overall fit.

entry.title: Let Them Peek: Group Sequential Designs for A/B Testing

link.title: Let Them Peek: Group Sequential Designs for A/B Testing

entry.content: Randomized controlled trials, commonly known as A/B tests, are the standard mechanism for inferring causal effects of product innovations. Standard platforms evaluate these tests with fixed-horizon procedures that control the false positive rate at a predetermined time, forcing teams to wait until the end even when early data strongly indicates success or failure. Unfortunately, continuous monitoring (“peeking”) invalidates these guarantees, while always-valid inference is overly conservative under a strict deadline, and group sequential designs (GSD) have received limited traction in large-scale experimentation due to operational barriers: terminal-rule preservation, autocorrelation, latent effect-size distributions, calendar-duration optimization. We fill in this gap by proposing a Predictive Probability of Success (PPoS) group sequential framework that is autocorrelation-aware and duration-optimal while preserving the platform’s fixed-horizon terminal rule. Our key insight is that PPoS thresholds map to closed-form lift boundaries that converge to the standard test at the horizon by construction, admit an effective-sample-size correction estimated from historical A/A tests, and suffice to attain the likelihood-ratio efficiency floor. Experimentally on online A/A and A/B experiments, we show that the proposed policy reduces expected duration by 43.1% (7.97 days vs. 14-day baseline), increasing effective platform capacity by 76%, while retaining the guarantees on FPR and power.

entry.title: Optimal aggregation in multiclass classification

link.title: Optimal aggregation in multiclass classification

entry.content: This paper studies the problem of aggregation in multiclass classification, generalizing existing results for binary classification. Given a finite dictionary of score functions F={f_1,…,f_M} and a training sample, the goal is to construct a data-driven aggregate whose risk is as close as possible to that of the best aggregate (oracle) in a prescribed subset of span(F) with respect to a given loss. In particular, we investigate model selection and convex aggregation under the 0/1 and multinomial logistic losses. For the 0/1 loss, we show that the optimal aggregation rates remarkably do not depend on the number of classes K, and the corresponding empirical risk minimization (ERM) aggregates are rate-optimal for model selection and nearly-optimal for convex aggregation (up to an additional sqrt(ln(K)) factor). The situation under the multinomial logistic loss is more subtle. Although the optimal aggregation rates remain independent of K, restricting aggregation to proper aggregates in conv(F) leads to a deterioration of the achievable rates with K in certain regimes. This reveals a fundamental limitation of proper aggregation in multiclass classification. To overcome it, we propose improper probability-mixture aggregates that average the induced class probabilities rather than the original score functions and map the result back to score-function space. These aggregates achieve optimal or nearly optimal convergence rates independent of K. Finally, we introduce a different aggregation framework in which both the aggregation class and the oracle are defined directly in probability space.

entry.title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning and Inference via Measure-Indexed Kernel Ridge Regression

link.title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning and Inference via Measure-Indexed Kernel Ridge Regression

entry.content: In-Context learning enables an estimator, trained across multiple tasks, to adapt to a new unseen task solely through its in-context samples, without any parameter refitting. Despite growing interest in the statistical foundations of in-context learning, two gaps still remain. First, existing convergence results do not characterize the distributional behavior of the in-context learning estimators. Second, classical nonparametric methods are not designed to handle the measure-valued inputs that in-context learning naturally produces. We address both gaps by developing a measure-indexed reproducing kernel Hilbert space framework, in which the adaptivity of the estimator is captured through the dependence of a mean functional on the empirical measure of the context. Within this framework, we propose a measure-indexed kernel ridge regression estimator computed from multiple independent tasks and establish its minimax-optimal convergence rate. We further prove that the proposed estimator is pointwise asymptotically normal, enabling the construction of confidence intervals for the mean and prediction intervals for the response on an unseen task. Notably, the estimator achieves valid uncertainty quantification without any refitting when adapting to a new task. As a special case, our framework recovers classical distributed nonparametric regression when all tasks share the same underlying function. The proposed framework is illustrated through a latent Gaussian process example.

entry.title: Quantifying the Threat: A Bayesian Probabilistic Framework for Heavy Metal Health Risks among Children in the Densu Basin, Ghana

link.title: Quantifying the Threat: A Bayesian Probabilistic Framework for Heavy Metal Health Risks among Children in the Densu Basin, Ghana

entry.content: Groundwater in Ghana’s Densu River Basin remains a key domestic water source, but multi-metal contamination threatens children’s health. Previous deterministic hazard index assessments provide limited treatment of uncertainty, co-exposure, and spatial variability. This study applies a Bayesian probabilistic framework for non-carcinogenic risk assessment using 94 groundwater samples and measurements of Fe, Mn, Ni, Pb, Cd, and As. A Bayesian regression model propagates parameter uncertainty and accounts for contaminant co-occurrence. Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is used for posterior inference, while inverse distance weighting generates spatially continuous risk surfaces. Pb, As, and Cd dominate cumulative risk. Posterior predictive results indicate that approximately 31% of sampling sites have a probability greater than 0.5 of exceeding a hazard index (HI) of 1. The risk surface is highly heterogeneous, with a posterior mean of 0.372 and a standard deviation of 0.416. High-risk zones often reflect moderate co-exposure rather than extreme contamination by a single metal. The framework provides uncertainty-aware, spatially explicit information to support groundwater monitoring, risk mitigation, and public health planning in data-limited regions.

entry.title: Efficient Bayesian Filtering and Inference for Integro-Difference Equation Models

link.title: Efficient Bayesian Filtering and Inference for Integro-Difference Equation Models

entry.content: Integro-Difference Equation (IDE) models are a class of dynamic spatio-temporal models which describe the temporal evolution of a spatial process, usually to model advection and diffusion of some random field over time. While several papers have focused on inference and performance of these models, little attention has been given to computational comparisons of various methods of computing posterior densities and performing inference. We address this problem in two parts. Firstly, in inference for these models, Kalman filtering (and smoothing) is often used; either to compute marginal likelihoods, or to sample from the hidden process conditional on the rest of the parameters of the model. There are many variations of the Kalman filter and smoother with substantially varying performance profiles and stability: the standard Kalman filter, its square-root form, its information form, to name a few. The information filters, when set up correctly, can compute the likelihood in $\mathcal O(nr^2 + r^3)$ time per time point ($n$ being the number of observations per time point), where the computation in $n$ can be done in parallel, on models with independent observation error. In this paper, we analyse these forms in the context of IDEs, considering computational speed and stability. Secondly, there are two main methods of inference used for the kind of dynamical system that IDEs can be reduced to; directly using the marginal likelihood without the hidden state, or constructing a block Gibbs sampler with the hidden state. We compare these two approaches in terms of computational efficiency and practical performance in the IDE setting. Using a block Gibbs sampler for inference on the system parameters proves to be more efficient in most cases, with a specific real-data example providing an exception.

entry.title: Likelihood-Based Confidence Curves for Bounded Parameters

link.title: Likelihood-Based Confidence Curves for Bounded Parameters

entry.content: When a parameter is bounded, the likelihood ratio statistic does not generally follow the chi-square limit distribution of Wilks’ theorem. In fact, its asymptotic null distribution depends on the distance from the null value to the boundary, interpolating between the chi-bar-square law on the boundary and the chi-square law in the deep interior of the parameter space. We derive this distribution and use it to construct confidence curves, which are nested collections of two-sided confidence intervals or regions, for bounded parameters. We extend the existing result for the scalar parameter to a two-dimensional parameter with one or both components bounded. As the bivariate distributions are integrals of normal distributions, which are not reducible to standard statistical functions, we also give a simpler approximated distribution obtained by moment-matching. We illustrate the methods on a canonical analysis from high-energy physics, namely the Poisson signal-plus-background experiment.

link.title: Bayesian nonparametric mixtures of asymmetric Archimedean copulas

entry.content: Archimedean copulas are exchangeable: a single generator parameter controls every pairwise association, and the copula is invariant under permutations of its arguments. Even when mixtures of Archimedean copulas are formulated, the exchangeability feature is inherited. Non exchangeable copulas can be defined through the Khoudraji transformation of an Archimedean copula. This relies in replacing the arguments by a power transformation and adding a factor based on the independence copula. The construction produces pairwise Kendall tau coefficients that depend on the power parameters and recovers the original Archimedean copula as a particular case. We propose a Bayesian nonparametric mixture model by mixing over the copula generator parameter and the parameters that characterize the asymmetry. We use the Poisson–Dirichlet process as a mixing distribution, which groups observations by both strength and direction of dependence. We derive the copula density, the pairwise association measures, the tail coefficients, and the full posterior conditional distributions to perform a Bayesian analysis. We carry out simulation studies and real data analyses. The results show that the Khoudraji mixture improves greatly on, or agrees with, the exchangeable fit.

entry.title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints

link.title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints

entry.content: Composite endpoints are common in clinical trials for binary, time-to-event or recurrent outcomes. Recently, there has been interest in estimands for continuous endpoints that employ a composite variable strategy for handling intercurrent events, whereby a value on the continuous scale is defined as the outcome. In this paper we describe these continuous composite endpoints where participants who experience the intercurrent event are assigned a pre-specified value on the outcome scale (which we call the failure value) instead of a measurement. We describe these endpoints and the difficulty of choosing the failure value when the mean is the chosen summary statistic. The large impact of the choice of failure value on the variance of the distribution of the endpoint is quantified as a function of the probability of the event and the standardised difference of the failure value from the mean of the unaffected values. Strategies for choosing failure values are discussed, emphasising the need to balance the clinical relevance and interpretability of the estimand with the need to reliably estimate it. Two potential solutions to situations where there is no relevant and viable choice of failure value are proposed; using failure values based on distributional characteristics to generate clinical relevance and using alternative summary measures to avoid the need to select specific values.

entry.title: Diversity, Efficiency, and Incentives in Political Prediction Markets

link.title: Diversity, Efficiency, and Incentives in Political Prediction Markets

entry.content: Critics of political prediction markets argue that prices are biased because traders are not representative of voters. We test this claim by analyzing data from political betting markets spanning more than 100 years. Our analysis yields two main findings: (1) Acros markets, traders were not representative of the voters. (2) Prices were not biased by political preferences of participants. For the 2024 election, we analyzed anonymized data from Kalshi, a CFTC-regulated exchange, the largest regulated political prediction market in the U.S. Kalshi’s traders were 86% male and half were under 30. In its first month of listing election contracts, Kalshi’s prices were more accurate than every poll-based forecast in the national race, the seven battleground states, and nineteen Senate races, and no poll-based forecast would have been profitable to trade against them in any group of presidential contests. Its volume came from areas that voted 28% Republican, while 60% of volume went to Republican positions. Traders with a single trade placed 73% of their volume on Harris. The association between a trader’s location and the direction of positions declines with trading activity and is zero among active traders, who account for most of the volume. Prices can be accurate with unrepresentative traders when the forecasts of profit-motivated traders do not depend on their demographics. Two other markets corroborate our findings. In New York’s 1900 market, bettors were older than the population and drawn from finance. On PredictIt in 2016, which limited each trader to $850 per contract, positions followed registered party more closely, as our theory predicts when market restrictions do not allow profit-motivated traders to set the price. Prediction market efficiency is driven by financial incentives over demographic representativeness.

link.title: Real-Time 24-hour Ahead Forecasting of Solar Energetic Particle Events with SEPNET-PRISM-R

entry.content: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events, operationally defined as proton flux exceeding 10 pfu in the >10 MeV channel, threaten spacecraft systems, astronaut safety, and high latitude aviation, yet continuous real-time forecasting with adequate lead time remains difficult. We present SEPNET-PRISM-R, a near-real-time system that issues hourly, 24 hour ahead probabilistic SEP forecasts. The model integrates multimodal solar data - including active region patches, flare features, coronal mass ejection (CME) characteristics, and historical proton flux - to concurrently predict SEP occurrences, peak proton flux, soft X-ray flux, and CME velocity, with the primary objective being SEP forecasting. entry.title: RECAP: Representation-Based Calibration with Amortized Pooling for Frequentist Simulation-Based Inference

link.title: RECAP: Representation-Based Calibration with Amortized Pooling for Frequentist Simulation-Based Inference

entry.content: Simulation-based inference enables uncertainty quantification in broad contexts when a simulation model is available but when a test statistic’s sampling distribution is not tractable. But, frequentist calibration in this setting can be costly over high-dimensional parameter spaces. RECAP pools simulated scores according to a representation that preserves this distribution exactly or approximately, allowing distant parameter values to share calibration information. Representations may be derived from model structure or learned independently. Empirical quantiles of the pooled scores then yield tests and confidence sets, for which we establish theoretical coverage guarantees. In the simulation studies, we show that RECAP has lower coverage error than existing approaches and power close to that of the point-wise oracle, while maintaining the computational benefits of amortized calibration. An application to population genomics illustrates learned low-dimensional calibration and interpretable uncertainty quantification.

entry.title: Interpretable subgroup identification across survival and generalized-linear outcomes

link.title: Interpretable subgroup identification across survival and generalized-linear outcomes

entry.content: A subgroup analysis searching a trial’s covariates or many prespecified subgroups often singles out a subgroup for its extremity, interpreted as if prespecified. Selection inflates the estimate; for a given selection rule, a correction removes the inflation. Two questions belong to the rule: which candidate to return, and whether to declare none. A third is whether inference extends to the patients left outside. We treat all three for interpretable subgroups, defined by conjunctions of covariate cuts, generated by forest search, a causal forest or a cross-fit surface estimator under one set of rules, each a modelling choice trading size against effect. Forest search screens candidates on splitting consistency, the rate at which effects replicate across half-splits; the screen is complementary-pairs stability selection in closed form, and the law of the maximum over the family gives the family-wise false-declaration rate when every candidate’s effect is at least a clinically specified benefit. Refit-free multiplier resampling gives adjusted one-sided bounds (subgroup and complement), joined in a two-subgroup claim, with coverage asymptotically exact under separated selection, characterized under local competition, and conditional on a family proposed from the outcomes. Two trial applications, and simulations built from them, cover survival, binary and continuous endpoints.

entry.title: Exact Covariance Structure and Efficient Computation for L-Comoments

link.title: Exact Covariance Structure and Efficient Computation for L-Comoments

entry.content: L-moments are useful summary statistics and so have been widely employed in statistical analysis. L-comoments provide a multivariate generalization of L-moments. Joint finite-sample covariance structure, which represents the sampling uncertainty, of L-comoments is less well understood than that of univariate L-moments. We thus derive exact finite-sample covariance formulas for sample L-comoments using explicit conditional U-statistic kernels. We further construct an asymptotic projection estimator and an unbiased estimator of the finite-sample covariance matrix and develop positive-definite corrections. An efficient rank-prefix algorithm evaluates the full unbiased covariance estimator in $O(n^2)$ time without enumerating disjoint subsets. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial computational savings. The results provide a basis for first-order covariance approximations for L-comoment ratios and for subsequent multivariate L-moment estimation.

link.title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels

entry.content: Sampling from a multimodal distribution is a fundamental and challenging problem in computational science and statistics. Among various approaches proposed for this task, one popular method is Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS). In this paper, we propose an interaction-based version of AIS by combining it with population-based Monte Carlo methods to improve its efficiency. By keeping track of an ensemble instead of a single sampler along some continuation path between the starting distribution and the target distribution, we take advantage of the interaction within the ensemble to encourage the exploration of undiscovered modes. Specifically, our main idea is to utilize either the snooker algorithm or the genetic algorithm used in Evolutionary Monte Carlo. We discuss how the proposed algorithm can be implemented and derive a partial differential equation governing the evolution of the ensemble under the continuous time and mean-field limit. We also test the efficiency of the proposed algorithm on various continuous and discrete distributions.

entry.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling

link.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling

entry.content: Nested sampling is widely used in astrophysics and cosmology to reliably infer model parameters and compare models within a Bayesian framework. To address models with many parameters, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) random walks are used within nested sampling to advance a live point population. Diagnostics for nested sampling inference are essential to verify that trustworthy astrophysical conclusions can be drawn. We develop a diagnostic to identify poorly mixed random walks that do not meet the requirements of nested sampling. The distance from the start to the end of the random walk, the jump distance, is compared to the typical neighbour distance between live points, to obtain a relative jump distance (RJD). A robust estimate of a typical neighbour Mahalanobis distance is obtained with the MLFriends algorithm. In mock and real-world inference applications such as inferring the distance to GW170817, we observe the relative jump distance. We propose the geometric mean and fraction of RJD>1 as new summary diagnostics. To evaluate the sensitivity of the new diagnostics, problematic runs are identified by comparison with reruns using much longer MCMC chains. Trustworthy inference runs are consistently associated with above 1.1, while problematic runs can fall below these thresholds. The RJD is more sensitive than previous tests based on the live point insertion order. The RJD diagnostic is proposed as a widely applicable diagnostic to verify inference with nested sampling. It is implemented in the UltraNest package in version 4.1.

entry.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference

link.title: Low-order outcomes and clustered designs: combining design and analysis for causal inference under network interference

entry.content: Variance reduction for causal inference in the presence of network interference is often achieved through either outcome modeling, typically analyzed under unit-randomized Bernoulli designs, or clustered experimental designs, typically analyzed without strong parametric assumptions. In this work, we study the intersection of these two approaches and make the following threefold contributions. First, we present an estimator of the total treatment effect (or global average treatment effect) in low-order outcome models when the data are collected under general experimental designs, generalizing previous results for Bernoulli designs. We refer to this estimator as the pseudoinverse estimator and give bounds on its bias and variance in terms of properties of the experimental design. Second, we evaluate these bounds for the case of Bernoulli graph cluster randomized (GCR) designs. Its variance scales like the smaller of the variance obtained by the estimator derived under a low-order assumption, and the variance obtained from cluster randomization, showing that combining these variance reduction strategies is preferable to using either individually. When the order of the potential outcomes model is correctly specified, our estimator is always unbiased, and under a misspecified model, we upper bound the bias by the closeness of the ground truth model to a low-order model. Third, we give empirical evidence that our variance bounds can be used to select a good clustering that minimizes the worst-case variance under a cluster randomized design from a set of candidate clusterings. Across a range of graphs and clustering algorithms, our method consistently selects clusterings that perform well on a range of response models, suggesting the practical use of our bounds.

entry.title: Data Sketching and Stacking: A Confluence of Two Strategies for Predictive Inference in Gaussian Process Regressions with High-Dimensional Features

link.title: Data Sketching and Stacking: A Confluence of Two Strategies for Predictive Inference in Gaussian Process Regressions with High-Dimensional Features

entry.content: This article focuses on drawing computationally-efficient predictive inference from Gaussian process (GP) regressions with a large number of features when the response is conditionally independent of the features given the projection to a noisy low dimensional manifold. Bayesian estimation of the regression relationship using Markov Chain Monte Carlo and subsequent predictive inference is computationally prohibitive and may lead to inferential inaccuracies since accurate variable selection is essentially impossible in such high-dimensional GP regressions. As an alternative, this article proposes a strategy to sketch the high-dimensional feature vector with a carefully constructed sketching matrix, before fitting a GP with the scalar outcome and the sketched feature vector to draw predictive inference. The analysis is performed in parallel with many different sketching matrices and smoothing parameters in different processors, and the predictive inferences are combined using Bayesian predictive stacking. Since posterior predictive distribution in each processor is analytically tractable, the algorithm allows bypassing the robustness issues due to convergence and mixing of MCMC chains, leading to fast implementation with very large number of features. Simulation studies show superior performance of the proposed approach with a wide variety of competitors. The approach outperforms competitors in drawing point prediction with predictive uncertainties of outdoor air pollution from satellite images.

entry.title: Scalable Bayesian Clustering for Integrative Analysis of Multi-View Data

link.title: Scalable Bayesian Clustering for Integrative Analysis of Multi-View Data

entry.content: In the era of Big Data, scalable and accurate clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data are essential. We present new Bayesian Distance Clustering (BDC) models and inference algorithms with improved scalability while maintaining the predictive accuracy of modern Bayesian nonparametric models. Unlike traditional methods, BDC models the distance between observations rather than the observations directly, offering a compromise between the scalability of distance-based methods and the enhanced predictive power and probabilistic interpretation of model-based methods. However, existing BDC models still rely on performing inference on the partition model to group observations into clusters. The support of this partition model grows exponentially with the dataset’s size, complicating posterior space exploration and leading to many costly likelihood evaluations. Inspired by $k$-medoids, we propose using tessellations in discrete space to simplify inference by focusing the learning task on finding the best tessellation centers, or “medoids”. Additionally, we extend our models to effectively handle multi-view data, such as data comprised of clusters that evolve across time, enhancing their applicability to complex datasets. The real data application in numismatics demonstrates the efficacy of our approach.

entry.title: Identifying Elasticities in Autocorrelated Time Series Using Causal Mechanism Graphs

link.title: Identifying Elasticities in Autocorrelated Time Series Using Causal Mechanism Graphs

entry.content: Instrumental variable (IV) methods are widely used to estimate the price elasticity of demand from observational data. However, naive IV estimators may be inconsistent in settings with autocorrelated time series. We argue that causal graphs taking into account time structure can simplify IV identification and help select consistent estimators. More precisely, we propose to model equilibrium conditions using causal mechanism time graphs. These (acyclic) graphs allow us to maintain the assumption of a simultaneous determination of prices and quantities and come with an interpretable notion of intervention. They further allow us to exploit recent advances in graphical inference to derive valid IV estimators that are consistent under weak assumptions. Finally, we argue that observing significant differences between the estimates of presumably valid estimators can help to reject false model assumptions, thereby improving our understanding of underlying economic dynamics. We apply our approach to the German electricity market, estimating the price elasticity of demand from simulated and real-world data. The findings underscore the importance of accounting for structural autocorrelation in IV-based analysis.

link.title: Robust Functional Ward’s Linkages with Applications in EEG data Clustering

entry.content: This paper proposes two robust linkage criteria, termed functional Ward-type linkages, for hierarchical clustering of grouped functional data, where each clustering unit is represented by a set of curves. Ordinary Ward\textquotesingle s linkage defines the cluster dissimilarity between two clusters as the increase in the sum of squared errors (SSE) upon merging, which can be interpreted graphically as an increase in within-cluster dispersion. Motivated by this principle, the proposed linkages measure the weighted increase in band width required to construct a common band containing the central representatives of two candidate clusters. To reduce the influence of outliers, the central curves are selected separately within each cluster by leveraging the magnitude-shape outlyingness measure and the modified band depth, respectively. Simulations and two EEG data analyses demonstrate the robustness and competitive performance of the proposed methods under a range of contamination settings.

entry.content: This paper develops an effective Bayesian approach to conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation in regression discontinuity designs (RDD), an increasingly prevalent form of quasi-experiment that facilitates causal inference. Earlier Bayesian approaches do not easily accommodate CATE estimation while recent frequentist approaches to this problem assume a known basis expansion, a steep model specification requirement that our approach avoids. The new model is a variant of a Bayesian additive regression tree (BART) model with linear leaf-level regressions on the running variable and a treatment dummy (and their interaction). The model adaptively partitions covariate space into regions where the slope on the running variable appreciably differs, providing interpretable Bayesian inference on conditional average treatment effects near the cutoff.

entry.title: Which Covariates to Adjust for? Specification-robust Causal Inference in Observational Studies

link.title: Which Covariates to Adjust for? Specification-robust Causal Inference in Observational Studies

entry.content: In observational causal inference, domain knowledge often leaves multiple covariate adjustments plausible, yet which of them satisfy ignorability is not testable. Different adjustments can yield conflicting conclusions about the average treatment effect, and standard remedies (e.g., adjusting for their union or intersection, or reporting the union or convex hull of the confidence intervals) can fail or produce confidence sets that do not shrink to a point with growing sample size. We propose a specification-robust procedure that returns a single point estimate and a confidence interval that is valid when at least one candidate adjustment satisfies ignorability, and has width shrinking at the parametric $1/\sqrt{n}$ rate. Our approach mirrors how trimming and overlap weighting handle overlap violations: We shift the target to a reweighted population, closest in KL divergence to the original population, for which credible, specification-robust inference is feasible. We also provide diagnostics to assess the population shift and an extension to protect any function of the covariates used for reweighting, similar to adding calipers in matching. Synthetic and real-data examples demonstrate that the proposed procedure provides substantially tighter confidence intervals than the convex hull while achieving nominal coverage for the new target population.

entry.title: Optimal product launch in uncertain competitive markets: A multi-agent adversarial risk analysis framework

link.title: Optimal product launch in uncertain competitive markets: A multi-agent adversarial risk analysis framework

entry.content: Product launching is a nuanced problem that entails choosing numerous decision variables, including timing, pricing, quality, and marketing strategy. Furthermore, decision-makers must account for multiple uncertainty sources. These include endogenous factors, such as product quality and the strategic decisions of competitors and consumers; as well as exogenous elements, like market evolution and regulations. This paper proposes a novel general framework to support product launch decisions in the presence of multiple competitors and buyers using adversarial risk analysis, mitigating the strong common-knowledge assumptions typical of standard game-theoretic approaches in this domain. We also introduce variants that account for multiple product purchases and integrate discrete choice models. To overcome the inherent computational intractability of modeling multi-agent strategic uncertainty, we deploy a simulation-optimization approach leveraging Bayesian optimization. Finally, we illustrate our proposed framework through a software launch case study focused on optimal timing, pricing, and quality decisions.

link.title: A nonparametric statistical method for deconvolving densities in the analysis of proteomic data

entry.content: Background: Genomic or proteomic data are frequently affected by noise or are convolutions of different biological signals. This is particularly relevant in skin aging research, in which intrinsic aging, driven by genetic factors, and extrinsic aging, caused by environmental exposure, are investigated considering the proteome of skin fibroblasts. Since all skin areas are affected by intrinsic aging, isolating the pure extrinsic signal from the mixture of intrinsic and extrinsic effects is crucial to investigate extrinsic aging. entry.title: Estimating treatment effects with a unified semi-parametric difference-in-differences approach

link.title: Estimating treatment effects with a unified semi-parametric difference-in-differences approach

entry.content: Difference-in-differences (DID) approaches estimate causal effects with observational data before and after an intervention. DID traditionally estimates the average treatment effect among the treated and assumes parallel trends in outcome means. With skewed outcomes, a transformation is often needed to compare means; however, transformations may be difficult to choose and results may be sensitive to the choice and must be interpreted on the transformed scale. Recent DID methods estimate alternative treatment effects that offer additional insights. However, each estimator requires a different parallel trends assumption. We introduce a new DID method that estimates average, quantile, probability, and novel Mann-Whitney treatment effects among the treated with a single unifying parallel trends assumption. The method uses a semi-parametric cumulative probability model (CPM): a linear model for a latent variable on covariates, where the latent variable results from an unspecified transformation of the outcome. Our approach makes a single parallel trends assumption on the expectation of the latent variable conditional on covariates. Hence, we avoid specifying outcome transformations and separate estimand-specific assumptions. We introduce the method; describe identification, estimation, and inference; conduct simulations evaluating its performance; and apply it to assess the impact of Medicaid expansion on CD4 count among people with HIV.

entry.title: On the analysis of sequential designs without a specified number of observations

link.title: On the analysis of sequential designs without a specified number of observations

entry.content: The paper focuses on sequential experiments whose outcomes, success or failure, can be expressed using a binomial distribution, and in which whether or not a further experiment is made depends on the prior outcomes. Examples include subsequent medical interventions until a target response is achieved. The maximum likelihood estimate of the treatment success probability is the ratio of the number of observed successes and the total number of times the treatment was administered. Despite a prespecified initial sample size, the total number of conducted interventions cannot be determined in advance, and the estimated total number of successes may not be equal to the one observed, so the estimated variance of success probability is not that of a binomial distribution. These results generalize to designs with a tree structure consisting of groups of the experiments with group-specific outcome distributions. The multiplicative models entailed are studied using the tools from algebraic statistics and the theory of relational models. The estimates of success probabilities and their covariance are derived and shown to depend on the structural properties of the relevant exponential family.

entry.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards

link.title: Optimal Cox regression under federated differential privacy: coefficients and cumulative hazards

entry.content: We study two canonical problems in distributed survival analysis under federated differential privacy (FDP): estimation of cumulative hazard functions and Cox regression coefficients, allowing for heterogeneous per-server sample sizes and privacy budgets. To quantify the fundamental cost of privacy, we derive minimax lower and upper bounds that match up to poly-logarithmic factors, revealing server-level phase transitions between private and non-private regimes. Our algorithms are computationally-efficient and are based on adapting differentially private binary tree and gradient descent algorithms to handle estimating equations with dependent terms. We also study three related problems: estimation of the cumulative baseline hazard and survival functions in the Cox model under FDP, and estimation of regression coefficients under the federated label differential privacy, a relaxed privacy notion. For these problems, we develop efficient algorithms, establish theoretical guarantees and investigate minimax optimality. Numerical experiments, including a real-data application, support the theoretical findings. The proposed methods are implemented in the accompanying R package FDPCox.

entry.title: Ensemble Control Variates

link.title: Ensemble Control Variates

entry.content: Control variates have become an increasingly popular variance-reduction technique in Bayesian inference. Many broadly applicable control variates are based on the Langevin-Stein operator, which leverages gradient information available from gradient-based samplers to produce variance-reduced estimators of expectations. These control variates typically require optimising over a function $u(\theta)$ within a user-defined functional class $\mathcal{G}$, such as the space of $Q$th-order polynomials or a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We propose using averaging-based ensemble learning to construct Stein-based control variates. While the proposed framework is broadly applicable, we focus on ensembles constructed from zero-variance control variates (ZVCV), a popular parametric approach based on solving a linear approximation problem that can easily be over-parameterised in medium-to-high dimensional settings. A common remedy is to use regularised ZVCV via penalised regression, but these methods can be prohibitively slow. We introduce ensemble ZVCV methods based on ensembles of OLS estimators and evaluate the proposed methods against established methods in the literature in a simulation study. Our results show that ensemble ZVCV methods are more statistically efficient than regularised ZVCV methods, while also being substantially faster. This work opens a new direction for constructing broadly applicable control variate techniques via ensemble learning.

link.title: Dynamic Prediction of Joint Longitudinal-Survival Models Using a Similarity-Based Approach

entry.content: Longitudinal and time-to-event data are often analyzed in biomarker research to study the association between the longitudinal biomarker measurements and the event-time outcome, in which the longitudinal information contributes to the probability of the outcome of interest. We propose a new similarity-based method for the dynamic prediction of joint models where we consider training the model on only a targeted subset of the data to obtain an improved outcome prediction. Through comprehensive simulation study and an application to intensive care unit data, we demonstrate that the predictive performance of the dynamic prediction of joint models can be improved with our proposed similarity-based approach.

entry.title: A Stable Lasso

link.title: A Stable Lasso

entry.content: The Lasso has been widely used as a method for variable selection, valued for its simplicity and empirical performance. However, Lasso’s selection stability deteriorates in the presence of correlated predictors. Several approaches have been developed to mitigate this limitation. In this paper, we provide a brief review of existing approaches, highlighting their limitations. We then propose a technique to improve the selection stability of Lasso by integrating a weighting scheme into the Lasso penalty function, where the weights are defined as an increasing function of a correlation-adjusted ranking that reflects the predictive power of predictors. Empirical evaluations on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Additional numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in stabilizing other regularization-based selection methods, indicating its potential as a general-purpose solution.

entry.title: A GNN-Based Approach for Code Smell Detection and Refactoring Opportunity Identification

link.title: A GNN-Based Approach for Code Smell Detection and Refactoring Opportunity Identification

entry.content: Code smells indicate latent design or implementation problems that may negatively affect software maintainability. Over the past decades, numerous approaches have been proposed for code smell refactoring, including those based on software metrics, predefined rules, machine learning/deep learning (ML/DL), and, more recently, large language models (LLMs). However, traditional metric- and rule-based approaches rely heavily on manually defined criteria, while ML/DL approaches are often constrained by the availability of training data and the design of model architectures. Although LLMs provide advanced code understanding capabilities, they typically incur substantial computational and time costs, particularly when applied to large-scale software systems. In this study, we propose a graph-based deep learning approach for code smell refactoring. Specifically, we construct code graphs at both the class and method levels and employ graph- and node-level classification to detect code smells and identify corresponding refactoring opportunities for three representative code smells: Long Method, Large Class, and Feature Envy. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated using SACS, a large-scale open-source dataset constructed through a semi-automated process. In the experiments, we implement the proposed approach using three representative GNN architectures: GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT. We further compare its performance with traditional refactoring approaches, an existing deep learning-based approach, and four representative lightweight LLMs. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the compared approaches across all evaluated code smell refactoring tasks, demonstrating that it provides both superior performance and greater efficiency.

entry.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains

link.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains

entry.content: We establish verifiable necessary conditions for central limit theorems (CLTs) of ergodic averages of Markov chains on general state spaces. Our criteria are based on discrete-time $\mathbf{L}$-drift conditions that can be verified through estimates for the one-step transition kernel of the original chain. They yield an integral criterion for failure of the CLT for a class of observables that includes unbounded functions and indicators of tail events. The main technical step transfers lower bounds for excursions of the original chain to regenerative excursions of its Nummelin split chain. The same drift conditions yield lower bounds on the tails of return times and modulated excursion functionals, on invariant tails, and on rates of convergence in $f$-variation and $L^p$-Wasserstein distance. These estimates apply without an explicit formula for the invariant distribution. Applications to unadjusted Langevin algorithms show preservation of polynomial target tail indices at every fixed step size. For Euler schemes with additive infinite-variance noise, we establish restrictions on invariant tails and transience under superlinear drifts. Schemes with linear drift, multiplicative noise and logarithmic innovation tails exhibit sharp polynomial convergence exponents and exact CLT thresholds, despite the absence of positive Euclidean moments.

entry.title: Calibrating hierarchical Bayesian domain inference for a proportion

link.title: Calibrating hierarchical Bayesian domain inference for a proportion

entry.content: Small area estimation (SAE) improves estimates for local communities or groups, such as counties, neighborhoods, or demographic subgroups, when data are insufficient for each area. This is important for targeting local resources and policies, especially when national-level or large-area data mask variation at a more granular level. Researchers often fit hierarchical Bayesian models to stabilize SAE when data are sparse. Ideally, Bayesian procedures also exhibit good frequentist properties, as demonstrated by calibrated Bayes metrics. However, hierarchical Bayesian models tend to shrink domain estimates toward the overall mean and may produce credible intervals that do not maintain nominal coverage. Hoff et al. developed the Frequentist, but Assisted by Bayes (FAB) intervals for subgroup estimates with normally distributed outcomes. However, non-normally distributed data present new challenges, and multiple types of intervals have been proposed for estimating proportions. We examine domain inference with binary outcomes and extend FAB intervals to improve nominal coverage. We describe how to numerically compute FAB intervals for a proportion and evaluate their performance through repeated simulation studies. Leveraging multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), we further refine SAE to correct for sample selection bias, construct the FAB intervals for MRP estimates and assess their repeated sampling properties. Finally, we apply the proposed inference methods to estimate COVID-19 infection rates across geographic and demographic subgroups. We find that the FAB intervals improve nominal coverage, at the cost of wider intervals.

entry.content: Generally, Lasso, Adaptive Lasso, and SCAD are standard approaches in variable selection in the presence of a large number of predictors. In recent years, during intensity function estimation for spatial point processes with a diverging number of predictors, many researchers have considered these penalized methods. But we have discussed a multi-resolution perspective for the variable selection method for spatial point process data. Its advantage is twofold: it not only efficiently selects the predictors but also provides the idea of which points are liable for selecting a predictor at a specific resolution. Actually, our research is motivated by the crime and accident occurrences in St. Louis and its neighborhoods. It is more relevant to select predictors at the local level, and thus we get the idea of which set of predictors is relevant for the occurrences of crime or accident in which parts of St. Louis. We describe the simulation results to justify the accuracy of local-level variable selection during intensity function estimation.

entry.content: Surveys that rely on ordinal polychotomous (Likert-like) items are widely employed to capture individual preferences because they allow respondents to express both the direction and strength of their preferences. entry.title: “Game, Set, Match”: Double Delight Watching a Grand Slam Tennis Match

link.title: “Game, Set, Match”: Double Delight Watching a Grand Slam Tennis Match

entry.content: Probabilistic properties of tennis scoring systems are examined and compared with best-of-K systems. A model, where each player has his/her own probability of winning his/her service point and which remains invariant for the duration of the match, and where outcomes of points played are independent of each other, is assumed. Probabilities of winning a game tie-breaker, a game, a set tie-breaker, a set, and the match are obtained. Since tennis scoring systems are unique, probability calculations require decomposing big and complicated problems into smaller and simpler constituent problems, solving these sub-problems, then combining to obtain the solution to the big problem. The problems that arise from tennis scoring systems offer excellent pedagogical venues for teaching probability, in particular, the use of the Theorem of Total Probability and the Iterated Rules for Mean, Variance, and Covariance. There are also many interesting questions in tennis, foremost of which is whether a tennis match under this assumption will actually end with probability one; or whether when two players of `equal abilities’ play a match, the first server possesses an advantage. These questions are addressed in this work. Tennis scoring systems are technically statistical decision systems to determine the better player. Since such a decision system is based on a finite number of points played, erroneous decisions could arise, such as the inferior player winning the match. We compare different systems in terms of the probability of the better player winning, as well as the duration of the match in terms of the number of points played.

link.title: Tiny but uniform improvements of adaptive BH procedures via compound e-values

entry.content: After the seminal Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) was proposed, dozens of papers have attempted to improve its power by adapting to the unknown proportion of nulls. We observe that most null-proportion estimates are simply compound e-values in disguise, and thus most adaptive FDR procedures can be interpreted as instances of the e-weighted BH (ep-BH) procedure of Ignatiadis, Wang, and Ramdas [2024], i.e., the BH procedure weighted by compound e-values. This lens helps us show that most existing procedures are inadmissible, and we provide uniform improvements to them. While the improvements are small in practice, they still come for free (without additional assumptions), and help unify the literature. We also use our “leave-one-out ep-BH method” to design a new method with finite-sample FDR control for the simultaneous t-test setting.

We study a generalization that comes from a Markov sequence of order p and a q-dependent sequence. We derive the relation of the model to Gaussian-ARMA models and to the Gaussian-GARCH(1,1) model. Additionally we analyze the copula moving aggregate process of order one, or MAG(1), as it is a basic building block. entry.title: A Causal Framework for Evaluating Jointly Longitudinal Outcomes and Surrogate Markers: A State-Space Approach

link.title: A Causal Framework for Evaluating Jointly Longitudinal Outcomes and Surrogate Markers: A State-Space Approach

entry.content: Surrogate markers offer the potential to reduce the burden of data collection by replacing costly or invasive primary outcomes with more accessible measurements, provided that they can faithfully indicate the effectiveness of a treatment. However, appropriate evaluation of a surrogate is particularly complex in longitudinal studies, where both outcomes and surrogates can evolve dynamically over time and interest lies not only in the treatment effect at one time, but rather treatment effects that may vary along the entire trajectory. In this paper, we develop a statistical framework for surrogate evaluation when both the surrogate and primary outcome are measured over time. Specifically, within the potential outcomes framework, we propose a formal causal definition of the proportion of the treatment effect on the longitudinal primary outcome that is explained by the treatment effect on the longitudinal surrogate. For estimation, we leverage state-space models, together with the Kalman filter and smoother, enabling efficient estimation of treatment effects under realistic conditions of temporal evolution and patient-level variability. We introduce a nonparametric bootstrap strategy for state-space models, a temporal homogeneity test, and demonstrate the finite-sample performance of our proposed methods via a simulation study and application to a diabetes clinical trial.

entry.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives

link.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives

entry.content: Materials science data collection can be expensive, making dataset reuse and long-term utility important for future discovery. In practice, data collection often prioritizes properties of current interest while other properties are excluded from the acquisition process. This can produce datasets that are well suited for current objectives but lose information needed for properties of future interest. Here, we present how to construct datasets that remain informative for both. We develop and evaluate acquisition frameworks that combine predictive disagreement with diversity in material features, predicted outcomes, or both. We test these approaches across four DFT datasets and an experimental thermoelectric dataset. Diversity inclusion in dataset construction can reduce present and future objectives trade-off by preserving a broader range of materials and property behavior during acquisition. Across all datasets, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II with disagreements and feature diversity (NSGA-II Dis. + diversity) framework developed in this work provides the most robust balance between current and future objectives. It maintains prediction performance above random sampling for current objectives while mitigating bias on excluded properties and, in many cases, improving their performance beyond random sampling. This diversity-aware acquisition framework provides a practical route to building materials datasets with unbiased quality entries and mitigating cold-start limitations in subsequent modeling and discovery campaigns.

entry.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments

link.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments

entry.content: Regulatory approval of products in high-stakes domains such as drug development requires statistical evidence of safety and efficacy through large-scale randomized controlled trials. However, the high financial cost of these trials may deter developers who lack absolute certainty in their product’s efficacy, ultimately stifling the development of `moonshot’ products that could offer high social utility. To address this inefficiency, in this paper, we introduce a statistical protocol for experimentation where the product developer (the agent) conducts a randomized controlled trial sequentially and the regulator (the principal) partially subsidizes its cost. By modeling the protocol using a belief Markov decision process, we show that the agent’s optimal strategy can be found efficiently using dynamic programming. Further, we show that the social utility is a piecewise linear and convex function over the subsidy level the principal selects, and thus the socially optimal subsidy can also be found efficiently using divide-and-conquer. Simulation experiments using publicly available data on antibiotic development and approval demonstrate that our statistical protocol can be used to increase social utility by more than $35$$\%$ relative to standard, non-sequential protocols.
